I take two tutorials each week:
| Day/Time | Location | Tutorial Code | |:------------------:|:--------------:|:--------------:| | Wednesday 1:00pm | The Spot-3014 | T01/06 | | Wednesday 2:00pm | The Spot-3014 | T01/05 |
- The software used for ECOM30004/90004 are **R and RStudio**, so these should be installed onto your computer as you will need them for completing tutorial tasks and assignments. - From Week 2 the tutorial will build on the lecture and self-directed activities from the previous week. You are expected to have attended or viewed the lecture and carried out the self-directed activities. - There will be a weekly homework submission following each tutorial, starting from Week 2. (more on next slide) ::: ## Tutorial Attendance and Homework (10% Assessment) - You should attend the tutorial you are officially enrolled in. - You must contact me in advance (e.g. by email) if you need to attend one of my other tutorial sessions. - Approval is subject to available capacity and obtained on a weekly basis. - **Starting from Week 3**, each week there will be 1 mark allocated if you *both* - attend the tutorial, *and* - by 11am Monday submit solutions to the previous week's self-directed activities on the LMS. - **Example:** the second self-directed activities will be first to be submitted, by Monday 11am of Week 3. ## This tutorial - This tutorial will revise/introduce some relevant R commands for this subject. - Introduce data on Retail sales for Australia that will be used for the first forecasting application in this subject. - Retail sales are considered a key indicator of the health of an economy, and are commonly a target of interest for commercial forecasters. Before starting with the questions, let's warm up by setting up our workspace in RStudio. Usually the first step is to set up the **working directory**. --- ### Warming Up: Setting Up Working Directory in R ::: {.callout-note} Setting up the working directory ensures that R can accurately locate where your data files are stored. It defines where R looks for files and where it saves outputs. ::: To set up your working directory, enter command: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} setwd("Your location goes here") ``` :::
Alternatively, you can click on: $$\boxed{\;\textsf{Session}\;}\;\;\to\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Set Working Directory}\;}\;\;\to\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Choose Directory}\;}$$ On my computer, it looks like: --- ### Warming Up: Checking Working Directory in R To check your working directory, enter `getwd()` into your Console tab: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} getwd() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "/Users/chenpengyun/Desktop/ECOM30004_Tutoring_2026/TSAF_Week1" ``` ::: :::
Your working directory is also displayed here (above the Console window):
:::{.callout-tip} If the folder looks correct, you can proceed to loading the datasets and files. ::: ## Warming Up: Some Useful Functions - To execute a single line of code: - To clear Console window: $$\begin{aligned} \textsf{Windows:}&\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Ctrl}\;} + \boxed{\;\textsf{L}\;}\\ \textsf{Mac:}&\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{control}\;} + \boxed{\;\textsf{L}\;}\quad\quad\textsf{(Note: not $\boxed{\;\textsf{Command}\;}$)}\\ \end{aligned}$$ - To recall the previous command(s) you have entered, press $\boxed{\;\uparrow\;}$ in Console. - To obtain help: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} help(aggregate) ?aggregate # Same as help() function ??aggregate # If you want to know which package it is from ``` ::: ## Question 1 ::: {.callout-question} Obtain the data file `RetailSales.csv`, and save it into an appropriate working directory. Read the data into an R dataframe. To get a sense of the variables in the dataframe, use the `head()` command to print out the first six rows of the dataframe. :::

::: {.callout-note} `aggregate` generates a new series, `Retail_q`, by summing up the monthly observations of each quarter. ::: ## Question 3(b) ::: {.callout-question} Create a window of this quarterly time series from 2000q1 to 2018q4, and produce a time series plot. :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} S_t <- window(Retail_q, start=c(2000,1), end=c(2018,4)) plot(S_t, main="Quarterly Australian Retail Sales", ylab="Retail sales ($m)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ECOM30004_Tutorial_1_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Question 4 ::: {.callout-question} Take the log of the quarterly time series and produce a plot. :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Y_t <- log(S_t) plot(Y_t, main="Retail sales (log), 2000q1 to 2018q4") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ECOM30004_Tutorial_1_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Questions 5 and 6 ::: {.callout-question} Denote the log retail sales time series as $Y_{t}$. Create the *first difference* time series $$\Delta Y_{t}=Y_{t}-Y_{t-1}$$ Print out the first six values of $Y_{t}$ and $\Delta Y_{t}$. What’s going on with the value of $\Delta Y_{t}$ for 2000q1? :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # First difference of quarterly log retail sales Y_t, convert to pct D_Y_t <- diff(Y_t)*100 print(round(head(cbind(Y_t,D_Y_t)),4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Y_t D_Y_t 2000 Q1 10.3685 NA 2000 Q2 10.4144 4.5997 2000 Q3 10.4116 -0.2842 2000 Q4 10.5805 16.8887 2001 Q1 10.4393 -14.1158 2001 Q2 10.4745 3.5186 ``` ::: :::
::: {.callout-note} The first value in `D_Y_t` is missing (`NA`) because there is no value of `Y_t` available before 10.3685 to compute the difference. Taking a difference of a time series will necessarily result in a shorter time series because of this. ::: ## Question 7 ::: {.callout-question} Denote the quarterly retail sales time series by $S_{t}$. Create a time series of the quarterly percentage change (growth rate) of this time series, that is $$R_{t}=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\times 100\%.$$ Compare the values of $\Delta Y_{t}$ and $R_{t}$. :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Percentage change of retail sales R_t <- diff(S_t)/lag(S_t,-1)*100 # Compare print(round(head(cbind(D_Y_t, R_t)),4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` D_Y_t R_t 2000 Q2 4.5997 4.7071 2000 Q3 -0.2842 -0.2838 2000 Q4 16.8887 18.3986 2001 Q1 -14.1158 -13.1648 2001 Q2 3.5186 3.5813 2001 Q3 2.2103 2.2349 ``` ::: ::: ## Question 7 ::: {.callout-question} Denote the quarterly retail sales time series by $S_{t}$. Create a time series of the quarterly percentage change (growth rate) of this time series, that is $$R_{t}=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\times 100\%.$$ Compare the values of $\Delta Y_{t}$ and $R_{t}$. :::
What does `lag(S_t, -1)` function do? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print(head(cbind(lag(S_t,-1),S_t))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` lag(S_t, -1) S_t 2000 Q1 NA 31839.1 2000 Q2 31839.1 33337.8 2000 Q3 33337.8 33243.2 2000 Q4 33243.2 39359.5 2001 Q1 39359.5 34177.9 2001 Q2 34177.9 35401.9 ``` ::: ::: ## Question 7 ctd: Why the comparison? :::{.incremental} - Adding 1 on both sides and take logs: \begin{align} R_{t}&=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\\ 1+R_{t}&=\frac{S_{t}}{S_{t-1}}\\ \log(1+R_{t})&=\log(S_{t})-\log(S_{t-1})\\ \log(1+R_{t})&=Y_{t}-Y_{t-1}\equiv\Delta Y_{t} \end{align} - Then with the approximation $\log(1+R_{t})\approx R_{t}$ for small values of $R_{t}$, we have $R_{t}\approx \Delta Y_{t}$: $$\text{$R_{t}\approx\log(1+R_{t})$}= \Delta Y_{t}$$ ::: ## Question 7 continued Why is $\ln(1+x)\approx x$ for small values of $x$?
## Question 7 ctd: Some further observations (1/2) ::: {.callout-question} Denote the quarterly retail sales time series by $S_{t}$. Create a time series of the quarterly percentage change (growth rate) of this time series, $R_{t}=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\times 100\%$. Compare the values of $\Delta Y_{t}$ and $R_{t}$. :::
::: {.callout-note} The values of $\log S_{t}-\log S_{t-1}$ and $R_{t}=(S_{t}-S_{t-1})/S_{t-1}$ are quite similar especially for the smaller changes. :::
For the entire time series the two variables are very highly correlated: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print(cor(R_t, D_Y_t)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.9985674 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} print(round(cor(R_t, D_Y_t), 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.999 ``` ::: ::: ## Question 7 ctd: Some further observations (2/2) ::: {.callout-note} The values of $\log S_{t}-\log S_{t-1}$ and $R_{t}=(S_{t}-S_{t-1})/S_{t-1}$ are quite similar especially for the smaller changes. :::
This is also evident in the plot shown below: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(as.numeric(R_t), as.numeric(D_Y_t), pch=16, cex=0.7, xlab="Rt", ylab="DYt") lines(as.numeric(R_t), as.numeric(R_t), col="blue") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ECOM30004_Tutorial_1_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Question 7 ctd: Why taking logs differences? - Taking log differences or simple returns is a common type of "filtering" in time series analysis. - Filtering tends to stablise/linearise features such as trend and seasonality. - Changes in a logged time series can be interpreted as approximately percentage changes, which is often convenient. - Also, time series models, such as AR models and VAR models, requires data to be *stationary* $\to$ filtering/transformation ensures this requirement is met. ## {data-background-color="#000F46"}
Thank you for coming!
